subject: St John Chrysostom

text_used.text: Every English quotation below was checked by script (case-insensitive, whitespace and CCEL footnote marks removed) against texts fetched whole and saved in design/saints-hub/sources/people/john-chrysostom/. Chrysostom's own works: the NPNF First Series (vol. 9 Stephens and others, 1889; vol. 10 Prevost rev. Riddle, 1888; vol. 11 Walker, Sheppard and Browne, 1889; vol. 12 Chambers, 1889; vol. 13 Alexander, Broadus and others, 1889; vol. 14 Marriott rev. Schaff, 1889), checked twice: in CCEL's unrevised plain text (ccel-npnf109 to 114) and in New Advent's revised pages (na-*.txt). Where New Advent modernises (thee/thou/ye become you), both forms are given: 'exact' is the form at the URL given, 'exact_unrevised' is CCEL's. The historians: Socrates and Sozomen (NPNF2 vol. 2, 1890), Theodoret and Jerome (NPNF2 vol. 3, 1892), Cassian (NPNF2 vol. 11, 1894), all checked in CCEL and New Advent. His first biography: Palladius, Dialogue concerning the Life of St John Chrysostom, tr. Herbert Moore (London, SPCK, 1921), tertullian.org transcription marked public domain (published before 1929, so public domain in the US). The Lazarus sermon: F. Allen, Four Discourses of Chrysostom (London, 1869), tertullian.org.
text_used.source: CCEL plain-text volumes npnf109-114, npnf202, npnf203, npnf211; New Advent; tertullian.org (Moore 1921, Allen 1869)
text_used.note: Display rule: capitals for every pronoun for God are already present in these translations for the lines chosen (e.g. 'Neglect Him not', 'His house', 'blaspheme Him'); no line below needs a change for the rule except where marked 'display'. Section numbers are the NPNF/New Advent paragraph numbers, for the checker only; the page must show work and homily or chapter in words.

born.text: At Antioch in Syria, about 347. Antioch is today Antakya, in south-central Turkey.
born.source: Catholic Encyclopedia (1910), 'St. John Chrysostom' (C. Baur): 'born at Antioch, c. 347'; Socrates, Church History, Book 6, chapter 3 ('a native of Antioch in Syria-Coele'); Palladius, Dialogue, chapter 5 ('by birth a man of Antioch'); Britannica, 'Antioch' summary: 'Antioch, Turkish Antakya or Hitay, City ... south-central Turkey'
born.note: No ancient source gives a year. 347 is the usual modern date (CE 1910, OCA, Britannica, the Coptic synaxarium, the Greek synaxarion.gr). The Episcopal Church's Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022 says 'around 354'; Wikidata gives 349. Print 'About 347'. Britannica place page: https://www.britannica.com/summary/Antioch-modern-and-ancient-city-south-central-Turkey

family.text: His father Secundus was a high-ranking officer in the army of Syria. He died soon after John was born. His mother Anthusa was widowed at twenty and never remarried. He had one elder sister.
family.source: Socrates, Church History 6.3 ('son of Secundus and Anthusa'); Palladius, Dialogue, chapter 5 ('his father holding the office of military commander in Syria; an elder sister was the only other child'); Letter to a Young Widow, section 2 (NPNF 9): his mother was 'forty years of age of which twenty had elapsed since she lost my father'; On the Priesthood, Book 1, section 5 (his mother on refusing a second marriage)
family.note: Widowed at twenty is a calculation from his own words (forty years old, widowed twenty years); the CE, Schaff's Prolegomena and OCA all state it outright. On the Priesthood does not name her; Socrates does.

grew_up.text: In Antioch. He studied rhetoric under Libanius, the most famous pagan orator of the day, and was headed for the law courts before he turned to the Scriptures.
grew_up.source: Socrates 6.3 ('He studied rhetoric under Libanius the sophist, and philosophy under Andragathius the philosopher. Being on the point of entering the practice of civil law...'); Sozomen, Church History 8.2
grew_up.note: NPNF note to Socrates 6.3: it appears he had spent some time in the practice of the law.

died.text: 14 September 407, in a martyr's chapel five or six miles outside Comana in Pontus, on a forced march into a harsher exile. He was worn out by the journey and ill. Comana's ruins are near Tokat, in northern Turkey. He was about 60.
died.source: Socrates 6.21 ('died in Comana on the Euxine, on the 14th of September' in 407); Palladius, Dialogue, chapter 11 (the martyr's shrine 'five or six miles from the town'); Schaff, Prolegomena, NPNF 9, chapter 10 ('in his sixtieth year, the tenth of his episcopate'); Britannica ('died September 14, 407, Comana, Helenopontus (aged 60)'); Britannica, 'Tokat': 'Tokat stands near the site of ancient Comana of Pontus'
died.note: Tokat page: https://www.britannica.com/place/Tokat-Turkey . Socrates's 'Comana on the Euxine' is loose; Comana is inland. Sozomen 8.28 writes 'Comani, in Armenia'.

buried.text: First beside the martyr Basiliscus, in the same chapel at Comana. On 27 January 438 his body was brought to Constantinople and laid in the Church of the Holy Apostles. Much later part of his relics were in Rome, at St Peter's. In 2004 Pope John Paul II gave some of them back to Constantinople.
buried.source: Palladius, Dialogue, chapter 11 ('buried in the same shrine as Basiliscus'); Socrates, Church History 7.45 (27 January 438, 'the church termed The Apostles'); 1916 Roman Martyrology, 27 January ('it was afterwards taken to Rome and placed in the basilica of the Prince of the Apostles'); Letter of John Paul II to Bartholomew I, 27 November 2004 ('some of their relics ... return to Constantinople')
buried.note: The Vatican letter covers Gregory Nazianzen and Chrysostom together and says 'some of their relics'. How and when the relics reached Rome (the 1204 sack is usually given) was not checked in a primary source.

also_called.text: Chrysostom, 'golden-mouthed', for his preaching. It was a nickname given after his death; the Catholic Encyclopedia says it first appears in writing in 553.
also_called.source: Catholic Encyclopedia (1910): '(Chrysostomos, "golden-mouthed" so called on account of his eloquence)'; 'whose surname "Chrysostom" occurs for the first time in the "Constitution" of Pope Vigilius ... in the year 553'
also_called.note: The quiz data already says 'Chrysostom means golden-mouthed. It was a nickname.' In his lifetime and in Palladius he is simply John.

also_called.text: John of Antioch; John of Constantinople. In Russian, Ioann Zlatoust ('golden mouth').
also_called.note: 'John of Antioch/Constantinople' are descriptive; they are in the research file but no dictionary was checked for them. Safe to print only Chrysostom and Zlatoust.

also_called.text: One of the Three Holy Hierarchs, with Basil the Great and Gregory the Theologian (Orthodox, 30 January). The OCA calls the three 'Ecumenical Teachers and Hierarchs'.
also_called.source: OCA, 'Synaxis of the Ecumenical Teachers and Hierarchs: Basil the Great, Gregory the Theologian, and John Chrysostom', commemorated 30 January

also_called.text: Doctor of the Church (Catholic), one of the four great Greek Doctors.
also_called.source: USCCB readings page title 'Memorial of Saint John Chrysostom, Bishop and Doctor of the Church'; Catholic Encyclopedia (1910), 'Doctors of the Church': in 1568 Pius V's new Breviary raised 'the feasts of the four Greek Doctors' to doubles
also_called.note: Many sites say Pius V 'declared' him a Doctor in 1568. The CE words it more carefully: the Breviary of 1568 raised the four Greek Doctors' feasts. Say 'honoured as a Doctor of the Church; Pius V's Breviary of 1568 gave the four Greek Doctors a higher feast'.

status.text: A saint to Catholics, Orthodox and Oriental Orthodox (Coptic). Anglicans and Lutherans remember him too.

patron_of.text: Preachers. Pope Pius X named him the heavenly patron of preachers ('sacred orators'). Britannica adds orators and speakers, education, and people with epilepsy.
patron_of.source: 1916 Roman Martyrology, 27 January: 'This illustrious preacher of the Word of God Pius X. declared and appointed heavenly patron of sacred orators.'; Britannica FAQ: 'the patron saint of orators, preachers, and speakers. He is also the patron of education and of people suffering from epilepsy.'
patron_of.note: Wikidata lists 2 patronages (unverified). The year of Pius X's act (usually given as 1908) was not checked.

in_art.text: In Eastern icons and mosaics: a bishop in a white omophorion with black crosses, holding a Gospel book, with a short dark beard and a high, bald forehead. In Western altarpieces he is dressed as a Latin bishop, in mitre and cope.
in_art.source: The pictures themselves: Hagia Sophia north tympanum mosaic (late 9th century); Byzantine and Christian Museum, Athens, BXM 11598; Cranach workshop, Magdalen Altar panel (about 1520-1525). Schaff, Prolegomena, NPNF 9, chapter 9 (his appearance: 'small stature ... a large, bald head, a lofty, wrinkled forehead, deep-set, bright, piercing eyes, pallid, hollow cheeks, and a short, gray beard')
in_art.note: This is observation from the works named, plus Schaff (1889), who drew his description from later Byzantine tradition (he cites the frontispiece of Fronton du Duc's edition). No iconography handbook was checked. A Western legend also shows him as a naked penitent on all fours (Durer, Cranach): see misquoted_or_legend.

wrote.text: More than any other Greek Father. About six hundred homilies and commentaries survive, with treatises (above all On the Priesthood) and about 240 letters, nearly all from exile.
wrote.source: Catholic Encyclopedia (1910): 'Of none of the other Greek Fathers do we possess so many writings'; letters 'about 238 in number'. Schaff, Prolegomena, NPNF 9, chapter 12: '(2) About six hundred Homilies and Commentaries'; chapter 10: 'His 242 extant letters are nearly all from the three years of his exile'
wrote.note: Counts of letters differ: CE about 238, Schaff 242, OCA 245. Print 'about 240'. The 'about 600' is Schaff's 1889 figure; modern catalogues were not checked.

pronounced.note: MW's first form puts the stress on the first syllable. Respelling is ours from MW's symbols. Checker 2026-09-25: MW's second form is kri-ˈsä-stəm; its 'ä' is the vowel of 'father', so 'SAH', not 'SOS'.

roles.name: Monk
roles.line: Four years with an old hermit, two alone in a cave
roles.note: The hermit is named Syrus. The two years 'without lying down by night or day' deadened his stomach, and the cold impaired his kidneys, and he came back to the city. Checker 2026-09-25: Palladius says the two years 'deadened his gastric organs, and the functions of the kidneys were impaired by the cold'; wording corrected.

roles.name: Deacon
roles.source: Catholic Encyclopedia ('Very probably in the beginning of 381 Meletius made him deacon'); Britannica ('an ordained deacon in 381')
roles.note: Palladius: 'after serving the altar for five years' as reader, 'he was ordained deacon by Meletius'.

roles.name: Preacher
roles.line: Priest at Antioch for twelve years, from 386
roles.source: Palladius, Dialogue, chapter 5 ('For twelve years he was a shining light in the Church of Antioch'); CE (priest in 386; 'His chief task during the next twelve years was that of preaching')
roles.note: Socrates 6.3 says he was ordained presbyter by Evagrius; Palladius and the CE say Flavian. Follow Palladius and the CE.

roles.name: Archbishop
roles.source: Socrates, Church History 6.2 (invested 'on the 26th of February' 398); CE ('ordained Bishop of Constantinople on 26 February, 398')
roles.note: LFF 2022 says 397 (the year Nectarius died). 398 is the consecration.

roles.name: Exile
roles.line: Deposed in 403 and 404; died on the road in 407
roles.note: An exile is not an office. If the path must be offices only, stop at Archbishop and say the rest in the moments.

catholic.text: 13 September, a memorial in the General Roman Calendar. Before 1969 his feast in Rome was 27 January, the day his body came back to Constantinople in 438. The 1916 Roman Martyrology lists him on 27 January (the feast) and on 14 September (his death, his 'birthday').
catholic.source: USCCB, 'Memorial of Saint John Chrysostom, Bishop and Doctor of the Church' (13 September 2025); Calendarium Romanum (1969), historical commentary, 13 September; The Roman Martyrology (1916), 27 January and 14 September
catholic.note: Calendarium Romanum 1969, commentary (Latin): 'S. Ioannes Chrysostomus obiit Cumanae in Ponto die 14 septembris 407, die qua celebratur Exaltatio sanctae Crucis. Apud Syros festum S. Ioannis agitur pridie huius diei, dum Byzantini et Copti id transtulerunt ad diem 13 novembris. Romae vero, inde a saeculo XIII, S. Ioannes Chrysostomus recolitur die 27 ianuarii, in anniversario translationis eius corporis Constantinopolim (438).' Text: https://archive.org/stream/CalendariumRomanum1969/Calendarium%20Romanum%20(1969)_djvu.txt . The 1916 Martyrology on 14 September: 'The same day, the birthday of St. John Chrysostom, bishop of Constantinople ... His feast is celebrated on the 27th of January'. The current (2004) Martyrology was not checked.

orthodox.text: Three days, in every Orthodox church checked: 13 November (his repose, moved from 14 September because that is the Exaltation of the Cross), 27 January (the return of his relics), and 30 January (the Three Holy Hierarchs). Churches on the old calendar keep them 13 days later: 26 November, 9 February and 12 February. The Russian Church also marks 14 September (27 September on the civil calendar) as the day of his death.
orthodox.source: OCA, 'Saint John Chrysostom, Archbishop of Constantinople', commemorated 13 November: 'Although he died on September 14, Saint John's celebration was transferred to this day because of the Feast of the Elevation of the Holy Cross. Saint John Chrysostom is also celebrated on January 27 and January 30.' saint.gr 3021 ('Εορτάζει στις 13 Νοεμβρίου') and 3342, the translation of relics ('Εορτάζει στις 27 Ιανουαρίου'); synaxarion.gr sid 1168 (feast 13 Νοεμβρίου; repose 14/9/407; relics 27/1); azbyka.ru: 'Дни памяти: 9 февраля - Перенесение мощей; 12 февраля - Собор Трех святителей; 27 сентября - Преставление; 26 ноября'
orthodox.note: Unlike Martin, the Orthodox churches agree on his dates; only the calendar differs. The Greek 30 January entry was not fetched from a Greek source (OCA only). GOARCH not tried (blocked a checker before). One Greek news site mentions 15 December for his ordination as patriarch; not verified, leave it out. Checker 2026-09-25: Greek 30 January now checked: saint.gr, 30 January 2026 ('Άγιοι Τρεις Ιεράρχες'; reading list: 'Τῶν τριῶν ἱεραρχῶν Βασιλείου τοῦ μεγάλου, Γρηγορίου τοῦ θεολόγου καὶ Ἰωάννου τοῦ Χρυσοστόμου'), https://www.saint.gr/01/30/index.aspx , saved as sources/people/john-chrysostom/saintgr-0130.txt. The page now prints the Russian Church's 14 September (azbyka.ru '27 сентября - Преставление'), which the draft had left out.

coptic.text: 17 Hator in the Coptic calendar, the day of his departure.
coptic.source: Coptic Synaxarium, Hator 17, 'The Departure of Saint John Chrysostom' (copticchurch.net)
coptic.note: The Gregorian equivalent was not checked on a Coptic source; leave it as '17 Hator'. Optional line on the page. Checker 2026-09-25: The page's 'Is he a saint?' row said '17 Hator, the day of his death'; he died on 14 September (the Calendarium Romanum 1969 says the Copts, like the Byzantines, moved him to 13 November, which 17 Hator matches on the old calendar). Now 'On 17 Hator, in its own calendar'.

anglican.text: Church of England: 13 September, a Lesser Festival ('John Chrysostom, Bishop of Constantinople, Teacher of the Faith, 407'). The Episcopal Church: 27 January ('John Chrysostom, Bishop and Theologian, 407').
anglican.source: Church of England, Common Worship calendar, September (printed in ordinary roman type, which the page's key says marks Lesser Festivals); Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022, January calendar and the entry for 27 January
anglican.note: LFF 2022 PDF: https://www.episcopalchurch.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/11/Lesser-Feasts-and-Fasts-2022_final.pdf . LFF explains its date: 'Thirty-one years later, his remains were brought back to Constantinople, and were buried on January 27, which thus became the traditional date of his commemoration.'

lutheran.text: Missouri Synod: 27 January, 'John Chrysostom, Preacher'. ELCA: 13 September, 'John Chrysostom, Bishop of Constantinople, 407'.
lutheran.source: Concordia Publishing House (LCMS publisher), 'Complete List of Church Year Commemorations' (January 27, 'John Chrysostom, Preacher'); Good Shepherd Lutheran, 'Commemorations in LSB'; Evangelical Lutheran Worship, 'The Church Year' (archived renewingworship.org PDF, 2006): 'September ... 13 John Chrysostom, Bishop of Constantinople, 407'
lutheran.note: ELW PDF: https://web.archive.org/web/20060908112753/http://www.renewingworship.org/ELW/content/PDF/ChurchYear_asm_20060119.pdf . This is the ELW draft listing, the same document used for Martin; not checked in the printed ELW.

why_they_differ.text: He died on 14 September, which is the Feast of the Cross. So the Greek Church moved him to 13 November, and the Syrians to 13 September, the day before. Rome kept 27 January, the day his body came home in 438, until 1969, when it took 13 September.
why_they_differ.source: Calendarium Romanum (1969), commentary on 13 September; OCA 13 November life; LFF 2022, 27 January
why_they_differ.note: Calendar order for the page. West: 27 January (Episcopal, LCMS; the pre-1969 Roman feast), 13 September (Catholic, Church of England, ELCA). East: 27 January, 30 January, 13 November (plus old-calendar note).

numbers.source: Palladius, Dialogue, chapter 5 ('For twelve years he was a shining light in the Church of Antioch'); CE (386; 'the next twelve years')
numbers.note: 'usually twice a week, but sometimes daily' is OCA's line; drop it if only ancient sources are wanted.

numbers.source: Schaff, Prolegomena, NPNF 9, chapter 12 ('About six hundred Homilies and Commentaries'); CE ('the ninety homilies on "St. Matthew"')
Stephens, introduction to the Letters to Olympias, NPNF 9 ('seventeen of Chrysostom's extant letters are addressed'); CE ('the seventeen letters to the deaconess Olympias'); Schaff chapter 10
numbers.note: New Advent prints only a selection.
Palladius, chapter 9: after 'only a single day' a catastrophe in the palace, and 'a few days afterwards they recalled John'.

numbers.source: Palladius, Dialogue, chapter 11 ('This most distressing journey took three months')
Schaff, Prolegomena ('Thirty-one years afterwards, January 27, 438'); LFF 2022 ('Thirty-one years later'); Britannica ('about 31 years later'); Socrates 7.45 (27 January, 438)
numbers.note: Socrates counts 'the thirty-fifth year after his deposition' (from 403); OCA says 'thirty years after'. 407 to 438 is 31. Other candidates: 'In a cave 2 years' (Palladius 5); 'Died at about 60' (Schaff, Britannica).

traits.title: a hot temper, and he knew it
traits.text: Telling how he dodged being made a bishop, he says people thought him 'the more hot tempered (meaning me)'. In the dialogue his friend Basil protests that John is far from anger; John answers that his calm came 'not by any innate virtue, but by my love of retirement'. A friend from his youth said he was quick to irritation.

quotes.exact: generally reputed to be the more hot tempered (meaning me)

Why then, my good friend, do you wish to bring me near the pyre, and to provoke the wild beast when he is tranquil? Are you not aware that I have achieved this condition, not by any innate virtue, but by my love of retirement?
one of his early friends has said that in his youth he manifested a proneness to irritability, rather than to modesty.

traits.note: New Advent quotes Socrates's friend with inner quote marks; CCEL has them as a single quotation. The personality test's Forge card and the 'love of retirement' line already rest on these. Checker 2026-09-25: Basil does not tease him about a temper. On the Priesthood, Book 3: 'who knows not how far removed you are from this infirmity?' John replies: 'Why then ... provoke the wild beast when he is tranquil?'

traits.title: would not stop saying it
traits.text: He told the rich of Antioch to teach their slaves a trade and set them free. Then he added: 'And I know that I am giving disgust to my hearers. But what must I do? For this I am set, and I shall not cease to say these things, whether anything comes of them or not.' A historian who admired him says it was his nature to rebuke wrongdoing.

quotes.exact: And I know that I am giving disgust to my hearers. But what must I do? For this I am set, and I shall not cease to say these things, whether anything comes of them or not.
quotes.exact_unrevised: And I know that I am giving disgust to my hearers. But what must I do? For this I am set, and I shall not cease to say these things, whether any thing come of them or not.

quotes.exact: He was naturally disposed to reprehend the misconduct of others, and to antagonize righteously those who acted unjustly

traits.note: The slave line: 'when you have purchased them and have taught them trades whereby to support themselves, let them go free' (same homily, section 6). He did not call for ending slavery; he allowed a household one or two servants.

traits.title: ate alone, gave to the poor
traits.text: As archbishop he cut the bishop's own spending and sent the money to the hospital. Then he built more hospitals, with doctors and cooks. He would not give dinner parties and ate alone, which his enemies called pride. His friend Palladius says he drank no wine, had a bad stomach, and counted money spent on 'men of pleasure' as sacrilege (Palladius, chapter 12).

quotes.exact: he erected other hospitals, over which he appointed two devout priests, as well as doctors and cooks
I admit that he used to eat alone

traits.note: Socrates 6.4 gives both explanations (a delicate stomach, or strict habit) and says 'Whatever the real motive may have been', it fed the charges against him. Checker 2026-09-25: Palladius, chapter 12: 'counting the expenditure of money on such people [men of pleasure] as sacrilege'. The page had 'feasting the rich'. That it fed the charges against him is Socrates 6.4.

traits.title: tender with a friend in trouble
traits.text: From exile he wrote long letters to lift the despair of his friend Olympias. He told her: 'pray do not deceive me by saying that you have thrown off all despondency'. And he begged her to look after her health.

quotes.exact: pray do not deceive me by saying that you have thrown off all despondency
quotes.place: the first letter in the NPNF selection ('To my lady')

traits.note: Also playful: after tricking his friend Basil into being ordained, 'I laughed for joy, and, seizing his right hand, I forced a kiss on him' (On the Priesthood, Book 1, section 6).

others_on_him.exact: "It would have been John," replied he, "had not the Christians taken him from us."
others_on_him.who: Libanius, his pagan teacher, asked on his deathbed who should succeed him. As told by Sozomen.
others_on_him.note: Reported speech; Sozomen wrote about 440. New Advent drops the inner quote marks. The best-known line about him.

others_on_him.exact: Remember your ancient teachers, and your priests; Gregory whose fame was spread through the world, Nectarius renowned for holiness, John a marvel of faith and purity.
others_on_him.who: John Cassian, who was ordained by him ('For I was admitted into the sacred ministry by the Bishop John, of blessed memory'), writing about 430
others_on_him.work: Cassian, On the Incarnation of the Lord
others_on_him.note: Same book, chapter 30: 'John the glory of the Episcopate of Constantinople, whose holy life obtained the reward of martyrdom without any show of Gentile persecution'. Both checked in CCEL npnf211 and New Advent.

others_on_him.exact: It is said that on account of his zeal for temperance he was stern and severe ... in private conversation he was frequently thought haughty and assuming by those who did not know him.
others_on_him.who: Socrates, a Constantinople historian writing about 440, fair but not a fan
others_on_him.note: The ellipsis joins two checked sentences of the same paragraph; the page could quote just the second. Balanced by the same chapter: 'In public teaching he was powerful in reforming the morals of his auditors'.

others_on_him.exact: This most distressing journey took three months; yet the saint among all these annoyances was always the same shining star
others_on_him.who: Palladius, a bishop who stood by him and wrote his Life as a dialogue soon after his death (the CE dates it about 408)
others_on_him.note: Also Palladius 11, what his enemies' own clergy said: 'Here is a formidable dead man, who frightens living men, and men in authority too, as bogies frighten children.'

life_moments.title: His mother's plea
life_moments.text: His father died soon after he was born, and his mother, widowed at twenty, raised him. His pagan teacher Libanius heard her story and cried out, 'Heavens! what women there are amongst the Christians.' When John wanted to leave home to live as a monk with his friend Basil, she took him into her room, sat by him on the bed where she had given birth to him, and begged him in tears to stay. 'Do not plunge me into a second widowhood,' she said, 'wait for my death.' He stayed.
quotes: Heavens! ... what women there are amongst the Christians.
do not plunge me into a second widowhood; nor revive the grief which is now laid to rest: wait for my death
life_moments.source: Letter to a Young Widow, section 2; On the Priesthood, Book 1, sections 5 and 6
life_moments.note: Libanius exact (CCEL): '"Heavens!" cried he "what women there are amongst the Christians."' The widow letter: https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1904.htm . The bed detail, exact (CCEL, On the Priesthood 1.5): 'she took me into her own private chamber, and, sitting near me on the bed where she had given birth to me, she shed torrents of tears'. The research file's 'sat him on the bed' is wrong: she sat. The same book (1.4) says that as a young man he 'attended the law-courts, and was in a flutter of excitement about the pleasures of the stage'.

life_moments.title: Two years in a cave
life_moments.text: He went to live with an old hermit in the hills for four years. Then he lived alone in a cave for two years. He hardly slept and never lay down. It wrecked his stomach and his kidneys, and he had to come back to the city. His biographer calls that the Saviour's providence, for the good of the Church.
life_moments.quote: Two years spent without lying down by night or day deadened his gastric organs, and the functions of the kidneys were impaired by the cold.
life_moments.note: Dates are not given in Palladius; the CE puts the monastic years in the 370s.

life_moments.title: The statues
life_moments.text: Angry at new taxes, the people of Antioch pulled down the statues of the emperor Theodosius. The city waited in terror for his revenge. Through that Lent John preached twenty or so sermons, calming and warning his people, until Bishop Flavian came back from the capital with the emperor's pardon.
life_moments.source: Catholic Encyclopedia (1910); Homilies on the Statues (NPNF 9); Britannica
life_moments.note: CE: 'a series of twenty or twenty-one (the nineteenth is probably not authentic) sermons'. Schaff: 'the famous twenty-one orations on the Statues'.

life_moments.title: Taken by stealth
life_moments.text: The emperor wanted him as archbishop of the capital. But the people of Antioch would probably have rioted rather than let him go. So the governor invited him to a martyrs' shrine outside the gates, put him in a carriage and sent him off under guard. He was consecrated on 26 February 398.
life_moments.source: Palladius, Dialogue, chapter 5; Sozomen 8.2 ('Asterius acted very prudently in sending for John before the citizens of Antioch knew what was about to occur'); Socrates 6.2 (26 February)
life_moments.note: Palladius names the gate 'Romanesia'. Theophilus of Alexandria consecrated him against his will (Socrates 6.2: threatened with charges by Eutropius). Checker 2026-09-25: Sozomen 8.2 says the people 'would probably have excited a sedition'; 'would never' overstated it.

life_moments.title: A consul at the altar
life_moments.text: Eutropius, the emperor's all-powerful chamberlain, had tried to end the right of sanctuary in churches. Then he fell from power and ran to the church himself. He clung to the altar while soldiers and people called for his death. The next day John preached over him: 'Vanity of vanities, all is vanity.' Eutropius was spared that day. He was later caught outside the church and put to death.
life_moments.quote: "Vanity of vanities, all is vanity"--it is always seasonable to utter this but more especially at the present time.
life_moments.source: Homily 1 on Eutropius, section 1 (NPNF 9); Socrates 6.5; CE
life_moments.note: In the same sermon he reminds Eutropius: 'I love thee better than they do who flatter thee?' (CCEL; New Advent modernises). Socrates says some thought the sermon added 'insult to cruelty'. Checker 2026-09-25: Homily 1 on Eutropius: the army 'demanded him to be given up for execution' and 'the rage of the people'; Stephens's introduction (NPNF 9): the sermon was preached the next day, a Sunday.

life_moments.title: Deposed twice
life_moments.text: Theophilus of Alexandria gathered bishops at an estate called The Oak. They deposed John for refusing to appear before judges who were his enemies. He was sent away, and recalled within days after a catastrophe in the palace frightened the empress. Months later a silver statue of the empress went up beside the cathedral, with noisy games. He spoke against them, and she took it personally. In 404 he was sent into exile again. His answer to the emperor's order was: 'thrust me out by force'.
life_moments.quote: I have received this Church ... from God our Saviour, for the care of the salvation of the people, and I cannot desert it; if, then, this is your will----for the city is yours----thrust me out by force, that I may plead your authority in defence of my desertion of my post.
life_moments.source: Socrates 6.15-6.18; Palladius, Dialogue, chapters 8 and 9; Theodoret 5.34
life_moments.note: The quotation is Palladius, chapter 9, exact apart from the ellipsis ('"I have received this Church," John sent word back, "from God our Saviour, ...'). 'Saviour' is not a pronoun, so no capital change. Theodoret 5.34 calls the catastrophe 'a great earthquake'. Checker 2026-09-25: 'Frightened the empress' stands on the Catholic Encyclopedia ('a sudden accident in the imperial palace, frightened the empress', citing Palladius 9) and Theodoret 5.34; Palladius himself says only that it 'caused such alarm'.

life_moments.title: The long road
life_moments.text: He was sent to Cucusus, a lonely village in Armenia, raided by bandits. From there he wrote to friends everywhere, fed the hungry and bought back captives. His enemies thought he still had too much influence. They had him marched towards Pityus, on the far shore of the Black Sea. He died on the way.
life_moments.source: Palladius, Dialogue, chapter 11; Sozomen 8.27 ('he purchased the liberty of many captives from the Isaurian robbers, and restored them to their families'); Sozomen 8.28
life_moments.note: Cucusus today is usually identified with Göksun, Turkey (not checked in a source; leave out). Checker 2026-09-25: No fetched source says 'mountains': Palladius 11 has 'a very lonely village in Armenia', the CE 'a secluded and rugged place on the east frontier of Armenia'. Removed.

summary.text: The early sources credit him with no healings or raisings, as Sulpicius does Martin. What they record are signs around him: a martyr who told him in a vision that he would die the next day, a catastrophe (an earthquake, says Theodoret) that got him recalled, a fire that his friend called heaven-sent, and a hailstorm before the empress died. The historians report these with their own doubts. The healing wonders come in much later stories.
summary.source: Palladius, Dialogue, chapters 9, 10, 11; Socrates 6.18, 6.19; Sozomen 8.22, 8.27, 8.28; Theodoret 5.34
summary.note: Proposal for the page: a smaller section than Martin's, titled for what it is (e.g. 'Signs, as the historians tell them'), with a 'Doubted from the start' box in the historians' words. The owner decides whether it belongs.

items.title: The martyr in the night
items.place: The chapel of Basiliscus, near Comana
items.text: On the last night of the march they lodged at the shrine of Basiliscus, a bishop of Comana martyred about a century before. That night, says Palladius, the martyr stood by John and spoke to him. John took it as a sure warning. The next morning he begged the soldiers to wait. They pushed on, but he fell so ill they had to turn back. He died at the shrine that day.
items.quote: Be of good cheer, brother; to-morrow we shall be together.
items.who_saw: John himself. Palladius adds, as a report ('It is said'), that the martyr had first told the priest of the shrine to get a place ready for 'our brother John'.
items.source: Palladius, Dialogue, chapter 11; Sozomen 8.28 ('It is said that during this journey, Basiliscus, the martyr, appeared to him ... and apprised him of the day of his death'); Theodoret 5.34 (buried beside Basiliscus, 'for so the martyr had ordained in a dream')
items.note: OCA renders the words 'Despair not, brother John! Tomorrow we shall be together.' (its own wording, unsourced). Use Moore.

items.title: The earthquake
items.text: The night after his first expulsion, says Theodoret, a great earthquake shook the city and terrified the empress. By morning messengers were crossing the Bosphorus to beg him to come back. The people lit torches and filled the strait with boats to bring him home.
items.quote: In the night there was a great earthquake and the empress was struck with terror.
items.note: Palladius 9 speaks only of 'a catastrophe' in the royal palace 'which caused such alarm, that a few days afterwards they recalled John'. Socrates 6.16 says the recall was because of the people's riot. The CE: 'a sudden accident in the imperial palace, frightened the empress'.

items.title: The fire
items.place: Hagia Sophia and the Senate house
items.text: As he was taken away for the last time, fire broke out from his own bishop's throne, burned the cathedral, jumped the street and destroyed the Senate house. Palladius saw the hand of God in it. He notes that the flames spared the small building where the church's treasures were kept, so no one could say John had stolen them, and that no one died.
items.quote: This clearly showed that the marvel was heaven-sent
items.note: Date: Socrates 6.18 ('on the 20th of June'). See doubts.

items.title: Hail, and the empress
items.text: That autumn, hailstones of huge size fell on the city. Four days later the empress Eudoxia died. Many took both as God's anger at how John had been treated. One of his loudest accusers, Bishop Cyrinus, had already lost both feet to an infection after another bishop trod on him.
items.quote: These occurrences were by many regarded as indications of Divine wrath on account of the persecution that had been carried on against John.
items.source: Sozomen 8.27; Socrates 6.19 (the hail 'on the 30th of September', the empress four days later; Cyrinus)
items.note: Told as the people's reading, which is how both historians tell it.

doubt.title: Doubted from the start
doubt.text: The historians who tell these things say plainly what they could not know. Socrates ends his account of the hail: 'God only knows, who is the discerner of secrets, and the just judge of truth itself. I have simply recorded the reports which were current at that time.' On the fire, he writes that 'some of the Johannites set fire to the church'. Sozomen says both sides blamed each other: 'The two parties mutually accused each other of incendiarism.' Of the parting prophecies between John and Epiphanius, Socrates writes: 'I cannot be sure that those who reported these things to me spoke the truth'.

cites.text: Socrates, Church History, Book 6, chapters 14, 18 and 19

doubt.note: All four lines script-checked in CCEL and New Advent.

later.title: A later story
later.text: Later accounts, told today by the OCA, say the soldiers sent for his body could not lift the coffin until the emperor wrote to John asking forgiveness, that the body was found incorrupt, that John opened his mouth in the Church of the Apostles and said 'Peace be to all', and that many sick were healed at his tomb. None of this is in Socrates or Theodoret, who wrote within a generation of 438. Theodoret tells only that the young emperor laid his head against the bier and prayed for pardon for his parents.
later.source: OCA, 'Translation of the relics of Saint John Chrysostom' (27 January); Theodoret 5.36 ('After first gazing upon the bier he laid his head against it, and prayed for his parents and for pardon on them who had ignorantly sinned'); Socrates 7.45
later.note: OCA gives no source. The OCA's own page says the feast of the translation 'was established in the ninth century'. Where the 'Peace be to all' story first appears was not checked.

feature.exact: Would you do honor to Christ's body? Neglect Him not when naked; do not while here you honor Him with silken garments, neglect Him perishing without of cold and nakedness.
feature.exact_unrevised: Wouldest thou do honor to Christ's body? Neglect Him not when naked; do not while here thou honorest Him with silken garments, neglect Him perishing without of cold and nakedness.
feature.context: Preached at Antioch about 390, on how to honour Christ in the Eucharist. A little later in the same homily: 'Do not therefore while adorning His house overlook your brother in distress, for he is more properly a temple than the other.'
feature.note: Tr. Prevost rev. Riddle (NPNF 10, 1888). Capitals already in the text. Greek not sourced. Alternative feature: 'Glory to God for all things', his habitual words and his last (Palladius, chapter 11); Greek 'Doxa to theo panton eneken' as transliterated in the CE (Δόξα τῷ Θεῷ πάντων ἕνεκεν, Greek script not checked against a Greek edition). Suggest using 'Glory to God for all things' in How he died and Homily 50 here. The Homilies on Matthew date: CE ('about the year 390').

lines.exact: remember constantly that not to share our own riches with the poor is a robbery of the poor, and a depriving them of their livelihood; and that that which we possess is not only our own, but also theirs.
lines.work: Sermons on Lazarus and the Rich Man
lines.place: Sermon 2, near the end (section 5 in the Catechism's reference)
lines.translation: F. Allen, Four Discourses of Chrysostom (London, 1869)
lines.context: His best-known line on wealth. The Catechism of the Catholic Church quotes it at paragraph 2446 ('Hom. in Lazaro 2, 5: PG 48, 992').
lines.greek: τὸ μὴ μεταδιδόναι πένησιν ἐκ τῶν οἰκείων χρημάτων, ἁρπαγὴ πενήτων ἐστὶ καὶ ἀποστέρησις τῆς ἐκείνων ζωῆς· καὶ οὐ τὰ ἡμέτερα, ἀλλὰ τὰ ἐκείνων κατέχομεν.
lines.note: Allen softens the end: the Greek says 'we hold not what is ours, but what is theirs', where Allen has 'not only our own, but also theirs'. The site's own translation in the quiz ('What we hold on to is not ours, but theirs') follows the Greek more closely. Greek checked on a substack reproduction of Migne (https://andreasfotiadis68agiosminas.substack.com/p/saint-john-chrysostom-second-discourse), not on a scan of PG 48. CCC: https://www.vatican.va/archive/ENG0015/__P8F.HTM

lines.exact: Mercy is called by that name for this reason, that it gives even to the unworthy.
lines.work: Sermons on Lazarus and the Rich Man
lines.context: Against checking whether a beggar deserves help. Same sermon: 'It becomes him that is truly well-disposed not to require an account of a man's past life, but simply to relieve poverty and to satisfy want.'

lines.exact: For there is only one thing, Olympias, which is really terrible, only one real trial, and that is sin
lines.place: the first letter in the NPNF selection, section 1
lines.context: Written from exile to his grieving friend.

lines.exact: I do not think there are many among Bishops that will be saved, but many more that perish: and the reason is, that it is an affair that requires a great mind.
lines.context: On the weight of being a bishop. The real source of the often-quoted 'skulls of bishops' line (see misquoted).

lines.exact: Why, this is what has ruined all, your supposing that the reading of the divine Scriptures appertains to those only, when you need it much more than they.
lines.exact_unrevised: Why, this is what hath ruined all, your supposing that the reading of the divine Scriptures appertains to those only, when ye need it much more than they.
lines.context: To people who said Bible reading was for monks.
lines.note: He goes on: 'For they that dwell in the world, and each day receive wounds, these have most need of medicines.'

lines.exact: You both have become one man, one living creature; and do you still say my own? Cursed and abominable word that it is, it was brought in by the devil.
lines.exact_unrevised: ye both are become one man, one living creature; and dost thou still say "mine own"? cursed and abominable word that it is, it was brought in by the devil.
lines.context: To husbands and wives who kept their money apart.

lines.exact: Tempers are wanted, not talking; character, not cleverness; deeds, not words.
lines.context: On raising children: aim for good character, not a clever speaker. Said by a man trained by the best orator of his age.

lines.exact: attempt, sir, no such promise, nor order what is holy to be given to the dogs. I will never suffer the worshippers and praisers of the Divine Word to be expelled and their church to be given to them that blaspheme Him.
lines.context: To the emperor Arcadius, who wanted to give a church to the Arian general Gainas to keep him quiet. As Theodoret reports it (about 450).
lines.note: Reported speech; the first sentence is script-checked and the second read in the same passage (CCEL line 15709-15712). Theodoret's text opens with '"But," said that noble man, "attempt, sir...'

misquoted_or_legend.claim: "He who is not angry when he has cause, sins."
misquoted_or_legend.truth: Not his. It comes from the Opus Imperfectum on Matthew, a fifth-century commentary by an Arian writer that was long printed with his works. Aquinas quotes it as Chrysostom's; New Advent's edition of the Summa marks it 'falsely ascribed to St. John Chrysostom'.
misquoted_or_legend.source: Summa Theologiae II-II, question 158, article 8, 'On the contrary' ('Chrysostom [Hom. xi in Matth. in the Opus Imperfectum, falsely ascribed to St. John Chrysostom] says: "He who is not angry, whereas he has cause to be, sins."'); Catholic Encyclopedia ('The most important spurious work in Latin is the "Opus imperfectum", written by an Arian in the first half of the fifth century')
misquoted_or_legend.note: His real line on anger (the quiz shows it): Homily 16 on Matthew, section 9.

misquoted_or_legend.claim: "If you cannot find Christ in the beggar at the church door, you will not find Him in the chalice."
misquoted_or_legend.truth: A modern summary. The words are not in his homilies as translated in the NPNF. The real passage is Homily 50 on Matthew: 'Neglect Him not when naked...' and 'he is more properly a temple than the other'.
misquoted_or_legend.source: Search of the NPNF First Series vols. 9-14 (CCEL plain text) for 'church door' and 'in the chalice': no such sentence; Homilies on Matthew, Homily 50, sections 4-5
misquoted_or_legend.note: The NPNF is not the whole of his works (e.g. the Genesis and Psalms homilies are missing). Say 'not found in his works in English' only with that caveat; safer: 'Not his words. The idea is his, in Homily 50 on Matthew.'

misquoted_or_legend.claim: "The road to hell is paved with the skulls of priests" (or 'the floor of hell ... bishops').
misquoted_or_legend.truth: No such line in his homilies in the NPNF. What he did say is milder: 'I do not think there are many among Bishops that will be saved, but many more that perish'.
misquoted_or_legend.source: Search of NPNF1 vols. 9-14 for 'skull' and 'paved' (no match in this sense); Homilies on Acts, Homily 3
misquoted_or_legend.note: No Quote Investigator page found; not searched further.

misquoted_or_legend.claim: He preached a sermon that began, "Again Herodias raves; again she is troubled; she dances again..."
misquoted_or_legend.truth: Socrates and Sozomen report that he opened a sermon that way against the empress. The sermon that survives with those words is rejected as not his. So it is 'reported by Socrates', not a text of his.
misquoted_or_legend.source: Socrates 6.18; Schaff, Prolegomena, NPNF 9, note 18: the homily with this opening 'is unworthy of his pen and rejected as spurious by Tillemont, Savile and Montfaucon'; NPNF 3 note to Theodoret 5.34 ('generally rejected as spurious')
misquoted_or_legend.note: Schaff adds that it is 'quite probable that Chrysostom made some allusion to Eudoxia which might be construed by his enemies in that way'.

misquoted_or_legend.claim: He wrote the Divine Liturgy of St John Chrysostom.
misquoted_or_legend.truth: The Liturgy most used in Orthodox churches bears his name, but how much of it is his is doubtful. The Catholic Encyclopedia says he 'perhaps modified, but did not compose the ancient text'. Britannica calls the evidence 'unconvincing'. The OCA says he 'compiled a Liturgy'.
misquoted_or_legend.source: Catholic Encyclopedia (1910); Britannica ('the evidence that he had anything to do with its composition is unconvincing'); OCA 13 November life
misquoted_or_legend.note: Give both views; the Orthodox tradition holds the anaphora to be his.

misquoted_or_legend.claim: The 'Prayer of St Chrysostom' in the Book of Common Prayer is his.
misquoted_or_legend.truth: It was taken from the Liturgy that bears his name, 'hence the attribution of the prayer', says Britannica.
misquoted_or_legend.note: Where in the Liturgy (the prayer of the third antiphon) was not checked.

misquoted_or_legend.claim: He studied at Athens with his friend St Basil the Great.
misquoted_or_legend.truth: His friend Basil in On the Priesthood was a different Basil. Basil the Great was eighteen years older. Socrates took the two for one man. Some Greek and Coptic lives today send John to school at Athens beside Basil; no early Life says so.
misquoted_or_legend.source: NPNF 2 note to Socrates 6.3: 'Socrates and Kurtz ... confound this Basil with Basil the Great of Cappadocia, who was eighteen years older than Chrysostom, and died in 379'; synaxarion.gr sid 1168 ('σπούδασε ... στὴν Ἀθήνα, μαζὶ μὲ τὸν ἀγαπημένο του φίλο Μ. Βασίλειο'); Coptic Synaxarium, Hator 17 ('He went to the city of Athens')
misquoted_or_legend.note: Palladius and Socrates place his schooling at Antioch under Libanius. The friend was probably Basil of Raphanea (NPNF note, after Baronius and Montfaucon). Checker 2026-09-25: Socrates does not mention Athens, so 'the story spread' from him was an unsourced link; reworded. The Athens line is in saint.gr 3021 and synaxarion.gr 1168 ('στην Αθήνα, μαζί με τον αγαπημένο του φίλο Μέγα Βασίλειο') and the Coptic synaxarium.

misquoted_or_legend.claim: Pope Innocent I ordered him back from exile.
misquoted_or_legend.truth: The 1916 Roman Martyrology says he 'was recalled by a decree of the Sovereign Pontiff, Innocent I'. The historians say Innocent tried: he sent bishops east to call a council, and they were sent home in disgrace. John died in exile.
misquoted_or_legend.source: 1916 Roman Martyrology, 14 September; Sozomen 8.28; Palladius, chapters 3-4; Britannica ('the pope attempted to intervene, but his efforts were brought to nothing')
misquoted_or_legend.note: Good example of an official text getting it wrong; say it gently.

misquoted_or_legend.claim: After a sin with an emperor's daughter, he wandered in the wilderness as a penitent.
misquoted_or_legend.truth: A later legend, the 'Penance of St John Chrysostom', painted and engraved by Durer and Cranach. None of the early accounts (Palladius, Socrates, Sozomen, Theodoret) tell it.
misquoted_or_legend.source: Art Institute of Chicago, Cranach, 'The Penitence of Saint John Chrysostom' (1509): 'the legendary remorse of the great 4th-century Bishop of Constantinople, who succumbed to the attractions of the emperor's daughter and then wandered the wilderness in penitence'; our reading of the four early sources
misquoted_or_legend.note: API record saved as sources/.../aic-13612.json. The AIC page itself was not opened in a browser. Checker 2026-09-25: The Art Institute says he 'wandered the wilderness in penitence'; 'crawled on all fours' and 'naked' and 'medieval Western' are not in any fetched source. Reworded.

misquoted_or_legend.claim: "Approach, although you may have repented a thousand times."
misquoted_or_legend.truth: Socrates says he preached this and was attacked for it. The words are not found in any sermon of his that survives.
misquoted_or_legend.source: Socrates 6.21; NPNF 2 note: 'These words are not found in any of Chrysostom's extant homilies.'
misquoted_or_legend.note: Optional; interesting for the second-chances theme.

hard_topics.title: The sermons Against the Jews
hard_topics.text: At Antioch, about 387, he preached eight sermons usually called Against the Jews. They attack Judaism and the Jews of his day in the harshest terms. In the first he calls the synagogue 'a brothel and a theatre', 'a den of robbers and a lair of wild beasts', applying lines from Jeremiah. He says whom he is aiming at: members of his own church who went to watch the Jewish feasts and joined the fasts. Britannica calls his language 'certainly hateful and unambiguous', and says it was unusual 'even among his peers'. It also notes that 'some scholars assert that it is anachronistic to apply a modern understanding of antisemitism to a figure from the 4th century'. The standard English translation (Harkins, 1979) is titled Discourses against Judaizing Christians. In modern times the sermons have been posted by antisemites: the only free English translation online was first found on an antisemitic website.
hard_topics.his_words_greek: Ἔνθα δὲ πόρνη ἕστηκεν, πορνεῖόν ἐστιν ὁ τόπος· μᾶλλον δὲ οὐχὶ πορνεῖον καὶ θέατρον μόνον ἐστὶν ἡ συναγωγὴ, ἀλλὰ καὶ σπήλαιον λῃστῶν, καὶ καταγώγιον θηρίων
hard_topics.his_words_ours: Where a prostitute stands, that place is a brothel. Or rather, the synagogue is not only a brothel and a theatre. It is also a den of robbers and a lair of wild beasts.
hard_topics.target_greek: καὶ πολλοὶ τῶν μεθ' ἡμῶν τεταγμένων καὶ τὰ ἡμέτερα λεγόντων φρονεῖν, οἱ μὲν ἐπὶ τὴν θέαν ἀπαντῶσι τῶν ἑορτῶν, οἱ δὲ καὶ συνεορτάζουσι καὶ τῶν νηστειῶν κοινωνοῦσι· καὶ τοῦτο τὸ πονηρὸν ἔθος βούλομαι τῆς Ἐκκλησίας ἀπελάσαι νῦν.
hard_topics.target_ours: Many of those ranked with us, who say they think as we do, go to watch the feasts. Others even keep the feasts with them and share their fasts. It is this evil habit I want to drive out of the Church now.
hard_topics.source: Against the Jews, Homily 1, sections 1 and 3 (Greek, Migne PG 48, cols. 844-847, Greek Wikisource); Britannica, 'St. John Chrysostom'; Roger Pearse, preface to the online edition (tertullian.org), quoting Paul Halsall: the translation 'was on an anti-Semitic website [as a justification for current anti-Semitism]'
hard_topics.note: No public-domain English translation exists. The anonymous online translation (tertullian.org, from the Medieval Sourcebook) has an unknown translator (possibly C. Mervyn Maxwell's 1967 thesis), so its status is uncertain: do not quote it. Print our own translations from the Greek, marked 'Our translation', as the quiz does for the Lazarus line. 'Applying lines from Jeremiah': just before, he quotes 'the prophet' (Jeremiah 3:3, the harlot's face), and just after, 'a hyena's den' (Jeremiah 12:9 in the Greek Bible). 'Den of robbers' echoes Jeremiah 7:11 but is not cited there. Date: Britannica gives 387; the first sermon was preached before the autumn feasts (Trumpets, Tabernacles, the fast), which it names. Socrates 6.3 says he wrote a book 'Against the Jews' while still a reader; that is probably a different work, and it was not checked. Britannica: https://www.britannica.com/biography/Saint-John-Chrysostom ; Pearse: https://roger-pearse.com/tertullian/fathers/chrysostom_adversus_judaeos_00_eintro.htm Checker 2026-09-25: πονηρὸν ἔθος rendered 'evil habit' (was 'bad habit').

hard_topics.title: Temples torn down
hard_topics.text: As archbishop he sent bands of monks, armed with imperial edicts, to tear down the pagan temples still standing in Phoenicia. He paid the workmen with gifts from rich Christian women, not public money. In the same years he gave the Goths of the capital a church with services in their own language.
hard_topics.quote: John got together certain monks who were fired with divine zeal, armed them with imperial edicts and despatched them against the idols' shrines.
hard_topics.source: Theodoret, Church History, Book 5, chapters 29 and 30
hard_topics.note: New Advent spells 'dispatched'; CCEL 'despatched'. Theodoret tells it as praise; say so.

hard_topics.title: Slavery
hard_topics.text: He did not call for ending slavery. He told the rich to keep one or two servants at most, and to buy slaves only to teach them a trade and set them free.
hard_topics.source: Homilies on First Corinthians, Homily 40, section 6
hard_topics.note: Optional. Checker 2026-09-25: Homily 40 on 1 Corinthians also says: 'But when Christ came, He put an end also to this.' Both sides now printed. 'Let them go free' is conditional: 'if it be in care for them'.

where_he_stood.text: Fourteen lines shown in the quiz (cells without hide), each found word for word in New Advent's revised NPNF text at the URL below, and (except where noted) in CCEL's unrevised text. Four more positions are hidden but scored (learning, nature, deeper, calling).

rows.note: New Advent has no section numbers on this page. Identical in CCEL.
Identical in CCEL. Section 7: 'I would vote a thousand times over for accepting the former' (the life among people).
CCEL puts inner quote marks: 'make me not this cold reply. "What matters it to me? I have nothing in common with him."'
CCEL unrevised: 'But thou, who expectest a resurrection, on what account dost thou lament?' New Advent: 'But you, who expectest...' (a half-revised form; the site prints New Advent's).
Identical in CCEL. Written to defend his trick on Basil.

rows.work: Sermons on Lazarus and the Rich Man
rows.note: The site shows OUR translation. Greek checked (substack copy of Migne). The public-domain Allen (1869) text is at this URL; see his_words for the difference.

rows.place: the second letter in the NPNF selection (beginning 'Do not be anxious on my behalf'), section 1
rows.note: CCEL unrevised: 'I beseech thee dear lady, and entreat thee ... restoration of thy bodily health'.
Identical in CCEL. Fairness: he says miracles are 'not done now' because faith would be cut short, not that God cannot.

friends_family_rivals.text: His mother, widowed at twenty, who raised him and begged him not to leave her for the monastery.
friends_family_rivals.source: Socrates 6.3; Letter to a Young Widow 2; On the Priesthood 1.5

friends_family_rivals.text: The great pagan orator who taught him rhetoric, and said on his deathbed that John should have succeeded him, 'had not the Christians taken him from us'.
Ran the ascetic school near Antioch where John and his friends studied the Scriptures, reading them for their plain sense.
Took the young John under his wing, baptised him, made him a reader and later a deacon.
The friend he tricked into being made a bishop while he hid; On the Priesthood is written as their conversation. Not Basil the Great.
friends_family_rivals.source: On the Priesthood, Book 1, sections 6-7; NPNF note to Socrates 6.3

friends_family_rivals.text: A fellow student who left the monastic life to marry; John's letter brought him back, says Sozomen. Sozomen and Socrates identify him with Theodore of Mopsuestia; the CE puts a question mark.
A rich widow and deaconess of Constantinople, his closest friend; he wrote her seventeen letters from exile, and she was tried after his fall and would not give way.
Ordained by him at Constantinople, and loyal to him all his life: 'John a marvel of faith and purity'.
friends_family_rivals.source: Cassian, On the Incarnation, Book 7, chapters 30-31
friends_family_rivals.note: The site's pair text: 'Chrysostom ordained Cassian a deacon in Constantinople.' 'Deacon' is the NPNF editor's reading (npnf211 note 2552); Cassian says 'admitted into the sacred ministry'.

friends_family_rivals.text: A bishop who took his side and wrote his Life as a dialogue, soon after his death.
Bishop of Rome, who backed him and broke communion with his enemies until his name was added to the roll of departed bishops.
friends_family_rivals.note: Checker 2026-09-25: Theodoret 5.34: 'until the name of that holy man had been inserted among those of deceased bishops'.

friends_family_rivals.text: Consecrated him against his own wishes, then led the Synod of the Oak that deposed him.
At first she backed him: she paid for the silver crosses carried in his night processions. Then she took his sermons against luxury as aimed at her and pressed for both exiles.
friends_family_rivals.source: Socrates 6.8 (silver crosses 'provided at the expense of the empress Eudoxia'), 6.15, 6.18; CE

how_he_died.big: He died on the road into a harsher exile, on 14 September 407, at a martyr's chapel near Comana in Pontus.
paras: Soldiers marched him for three months towards Pityus, on the far edge of the empire. One guard was kind to him in secret. The other hurried him on through rain and sun, hoping he would die.

Near Comana they spent the night at the chapel of the martyr Basiliscus. John said the martyr came to him in the night: 'to-morrow we shall be together.' In the morning he begged them to wait. They set off anyway, but he fell so ill that they turned back.

At the chapel he asked for white clothes and put them on, down to his shoes. He gave away everything else. He received Communion. Then he prayed his usual words, 'Glory to God for all things', signed himself with the cross at the last Amen, and died.
He was buried beside Basiliscus. Monks and virgins came from Syria, Cilicia, Pontus and Armenia.

paras_facts.text: He died deposed and in disgrace with the court. Rome and the West would not share communion with his enemies until his name was added to the roll of departed bishops. martyrology_1916.exact: At Constantinople, St. John, bishop, who was surnamed Chrysostom, on account of his golden flow of eloquence. He greatly promoted the interests of the Christian religion by his preaching and exemplary life, and after many toils, closed his life in banishment.

prayer.text: The only prayer securely his is the one he said all his life and last of all: 'Glory to God for all things.' The 'Prayer of St Chrysostom' in the Book of Common Prayer comes from the Liturgy named after him, and is not known to be his.

hub_card.card_line_suggestion: The golden-mouthed preacher of Antioch, who told the rich the poor had a claim on their money, and died in exile.

personality_test.text: The Christian Personality Test names him first among the saints of The Forge ('Serious by nature, and at your best when there is something to do.'). His card: 'A friend from his youth called him irritable, and an admiring historian says it was his nature to rebuke wrongdoing. He preached so hard against the powerful that he died in exile.' (Socrates and Sozomen). He is also quoted three times: on the body (1 Corinthians: 'let all be eye or all head: will not the body perish?'), in the quiet leaning ('not by any innate virtue, but by my love of retirement', On the Priesthood), and on Barnabas and Paul in the Forge-Hearth opposites ('the one was more tender and indulgent, but this one more strict and austere', Homilies on Acts).
personality_test.note: Every claim on the card checks: 'proneness to irritability' (Socrates 6.3, a friend's report); 'naturally disposed to reprehend the misconduct of others' (Sozomen 8.3). All three quotations were script-checked in CCEL (npnf112, npnf109 Book 3, npnf111). Label it 'His personality type', 'Our reading, from the Christian Personality Test'. The live URL was not opened.

site_data_flags.text: people.chrysostom.cells.surplus shows 'Our translation'. A public-domain English exists (F. Allen, 1869), but it softens the Greek ('not only our own, but also theirs' for 'not ours, but theirs'). Keeping our translation is defensible; the page could show Allen beside it, or cite the Catechism (2446), which translates it 'Not to enable the poor to share in our goods is to steal from them and deprive them of life.'

people.chrysostom.hook: 'He told the rich that keeping their surplus from the poor was robbery.' The Lazarus line says not sharing is robbery; 'surplus' matches Britannica's summary ('what was superfluous ... ought to be given away'). Fine.

people.chrysostom.pairs.cassian: 'Chrysostom ordained Cassian a deacon in Constantinople.' Cassian says only 'admitted into the sacred ministry by the Bishop John'; 'deacon' is the NPNF editor's reading (and standard). Fine.

The research file (group-09) gives dates 'c. 347 to 14 September 407' and says Palladius wrote 'tr. H. Moore, 1921': both confirmed. It says the Herodias sermon was 'reported' by Socrates and Sozomen and the surviving one spurious: confirmed (Schaff note 18).
Wikidata (unverified) gives birth 349 and feasts 27 January and 13 September; it lacks 13 November. Use the churches' own pages above.

Lesser Feasts and Fasts 2022 says 'born around 354' and 'In 397, he became Bishop of Constantinople'. Both differ from the CE and Socrates (about 347; consecrated 26 February 398). Print the CE and Socrates dates.
LFF 2022 also quotes the Paschal (Easter) homily as his. Its authorship was not checked; do not use it as his without a check.

The date of the Byzantine Museum icon (BXM 11598). The museum page gives none.
The Gregorian equivalent of the Coptic 17 Hator, and whether the Greek churches keep 30 January from a Greek source (OCA only).

Whether the online English 'Against the Jews' (tertullian.org, ex-Medieval Sourcebook) is public domain. Translator unknown. Not used.
Cucusus's modern name (Göksun) and Pityus's (Pitsunda): not checked in a source.

tidbits.text: Some people in his day called another bishop, Antiochus of Ptolemais, Chrysostom for his fine voice; in 404 he was one of four bishops who pressed the emperor to drive John out
tidbits.evidence: Sozomen, Church History, Book 8, chapter 10 (na-26028.txt line 80): 'Antiochus had so fine a voice and delivery that, by some persons, he was surnamed Chrysostom.'
